children.text: Community health workers—frontline public health workers who are trusted members of the communities they serve—represent the most robustly evidence-supported health equity intervention for rural populations. A 2025 systematic review in the American Journal of Public Health identified 34 high-quality studies of CHW programs in rural settings, finding a median ROI of 4.8:1 (range 3.1–8.2:1) and consistent evidence of impact across chronic disease management, maternal health, mental health navigation, and social needs resolution.
Why CHWs Work in Rural Settings

The CHW’s effectiveness in rural settings derives from three factors that no clinical or technology intervention can replicate: trusted community identity (CHWs are from the communities they serve, with existing social capital and cultural competency), geographic persistence (unlike visiting clinicians, CHWs live and work in the community year-round), and care navigation capability (CHWs can navigate both the formal healthcare system and the informal community resource network simultaneously). In rural communities where distrust of formal healthcare institutions runs high, the CHW is often the only health system representative who has earned patient trust.

The CHW is not a cheaper nurse. She is a community member with clinical training. The difference matters enormously in a rural county where the hospital is seen as a place you go to die, not a resource you use to stay healthy.

children.text: The Sustainable Financing Problem—and How States Are Solving It

The most common failure mode for CHW programs is financial: they launch as grant-funded pilots, demonstrate strong outcomes, and then lose funding when the grant ends. The rural health systems and state programs that have built durable CHW infrastructure have done so by solving the financing problem through one of three mechanisms: Medicaid CHW service billing (19 states now have specific Medicaid billing codes for CHW services), FQHC scope-of-service inclusion (FQHCs that include CHWs in their scope of service receive cost-based reimbursement), or value-based contract integration (including CHW cost as a shared savings investment in AHEAD and commercial VBC contracts).

Kentucky, West Virginia, and New Mexico—three states with both significant rural health disparities and active RHT programs—have all codified Medicaid CHW billing within the past 24 months. The financial model is now proven: a CHW at a $42,000 annual salary generating Medicaid billable services at $45/encounter, with an average caseload of 80 patients and 6 encounters per patient per year, generates $21,600 in direct Medicaid revenue—covering approximately half the salary cost, with shared savings and avoided acute care costs covering the remainder.

FINANCING PATHWAY: Rural health systems in states with Medicaid CHW billing codes should pursue a 3-source financing model: (1) Medicaid CHW billing for direct service encounters, (2) SDOH screening quality measure incentives (MIPS), and (3) shared savings allocation from AHEAD or commercial VBC contracts. This combination can fully fund a CHW program without grant dependence within 24 months.

children.text: CHW supply in rural areas is constrained by the absence of training infrastructure. Rural community colleges are the most effective CHW training pathway: programs of 6–12 months, embedded in local communities, that produce CHWs who are more likely to remain in their home communities after training. Eleven RHT program states have allocated CHW training infrastructure funding specifically to rural community college partnerships. The average training cost per CHW—$8,000–12,000 for a community college certificate program—represents an extraordinarily low human capital investment relative to the 4.8:1 ROI.
Building a Sustainable Rural CHW Program
Check your state’s Medicaid CHW billing code status and billing requirements before program design
Partner with a rural community college for CHW training pipeline—train from within the community
Build the three-source financing model from day one; do not design a program dependent on grant renewal
Include CHW cost as a shared savings investment in any VBC or AHEAD contract negotiation

summary: Community health workers generate a documented 3:1 to 8:1 return on investment in rural settings—the highest ROI of any single health equity intervention in the peer-reviewed literature. This analysis examines the evidence base, the sustainable financing models that have moved CHW programs from grant-dependent pilots to permanent infrastructure, and the workforce development pathway that is producing CHW supply at the scale rural communities need.
title: The Community Health Worker as Rural Health’s Most Cost-Effective Equity Intervention: Evidence, Economics, and the Implementation Model That Scales
